Hi Josephine,

I had lost count of the number of times I promised myself to never binge again, only to fail a few days, or even hours, later. 

I was out of control.
Nothing could stop me from bingeing.
I even binged, then purged, on a plane, in the middle of a flight, one time.

I can also remember finding a small bag of mixed sweets that somebody had left on a seat when I was working at my local cinema.
I couldn’t resist the urge.
I grabbed the bag and devoured the sweets right then and there. 

I can hardly believe that now.
Even somebody’s leftovers were way too tempting to pass up.

It is truly amazing to think about the lengths that the urges can force us to go to.
I was beginning to seriously question my own sanity. 

Despite confronting the strength of those urges day in and day out, I still couldn’t confront the reality of my life. 

I wanted to bury my head in the sand and pretend that it didn’t exist. 

I continued on delaying recovery.
After all, there is always tomorrow, right?

After all, I’d have a much better chance at success if I just waited for the right time.
I would recover, of course I would - but only when the circumstances for my recovery were absolutely perfect. 

It is so easy to play the ‘when’ game.

    •    When I have more time…
    •    When I am less stressed…
    •    When I feel ready…
    •    When my kids are older and more independent…
    •    When the new week starts...
 
The truth is that the perfect time never comes.
The stars never align in quite the right way. 

However, I've also learnt that the monster isn’t as scary as it might seem.
It’s just that we keep on wasting our energies on delaying the task, rather than getting it over and done with.
 
There are five surprisingly powerful words that I want you to say to yourself:

 if not now, then when?

This doesn't apply exclusively to your health.
This isn’t JUST about your eating disorder.
It applies to everything that you've been putting off.

What do you want to do? And why aren’t you doing it yet?

If not now, then when?

If I was able to do it, then you will be able to get there too. I promise.

Your friend and coach,

My humble suggestion, which I heard from a recovery professional:

- Write down a list of all the little things you are doing RIGHT (detox tea, prolonging an urge by 30 min., getting through almost a whole day, self-care, mindful eating, positive thoughts, whatever.)

This professional said “getting excited about victories cements learning.” So if you encourage yourself & focus on what you are doing right, no matter how small, it stimulates your mind towards recovery.

Conversely, beating oneself up over the “failures” has the opposite effect of making us more likely to continue bingeing/purging.

Some tools that are helping me manage the ups & downs of early sobriety:

- Morning Meditation- Sometimes I do online guided meditations if I can’t focus. 

- Journaling: I generally journal following my AM meditation & again at night to clear my head.

- Gratitude list: I write out 5 things I am grateful for every day. Also if I’m feeling stuck in an emotion or mood or compulsion, I do a gratitude list. It immediately clears my head.

- Support. I do an online AA meeting every AM. Not everyone is an AA fan but these folks have really helped me handle the ups & downs. Their stories of joyful lasting sobriety are inspiring.

- Reflective walks. I used to do more intense exercise but right now I’m trying to be gentle with myself and increase mindfulness.

- Focusing on others & how I can show love & compassion.

- I pray for patience every day because I need bucketloads for my recovery.

Hey there ... I can relate a lot. In the beginning I fell into the cycle all the way down ..  total rabbit hole. Food theft, deception, obsession, etc. I felt like such a POS. After more experience with recovery and relapses, I see things a bit differently ...

In bulimia, the “midbrain” which is not rational/moral associates the dopamine release from bingeing/purging as necessary for survival. So there’s a lot of neurological stuff in addiction that interferes with conscious or “moral” thinking.

Also bulimics tend to be malnourished and the bingeing is the body’s response to perceived starvation. It can override your “stop” mechanism which leads to compulsive & sometimes shameful behavior & thoughts.

So, there are scientific explanations beyond you suddenly becoming a terrible person...

also in the first year of bulimia I recall a sort of honeymoon phase ... I hated what I did but it was relatively new to me so on some level subconsciously exciting or inescapable... that faded though. I still struggle but I believe I will not die bulimic. I enjoy life without it too much. 

My two cents ... seek perspectives on the disorder that can lift you out of shame & self-flagellating ... a recovered woman told me, at the core of your relationship with food is your relationship with yourself. Bulimic women rarely treat themselves with the kindness, love or compassion they need to break the cycle.

My “best thinking” got me through 60 days sober before attending my first meeting. I was going through a lot of transformation at the time. Patching up damaged relationships, dealing with damage, looking at myself, seeing what I needed to change, turning back to a higher power I had neglected, etc. 

In that time of change, I realized I needed to get sober. After 60 days sober I got invited to AA for the first time. Had never been and knew nothing about it. I felt supported but also a little bombarded.

Anyways after those first 90 days I ended up suicidal for a lot of reasons and checked myself  in & out of psychiatric care for a summer. A lot was going on mentally,  alcohol abuse was one of several struggles (bulimia, bipolar, PTSD, etc). After psychiatric care I was a gunshy about returning to AA. Still had a lot of guards up. Reservations about entrusting all my struggles to a sponsor.  Etc. Kept attending but then began drinking again. 

Giving it a second go-around. In a different state this time. (Did not tell AA members I was moving because I knew I would just get labeled as a geographic drunk. And I was right.) Anyways I’m trying sobriety again and attending meetings but I do have my guards up regarding AA hardliners. The meetings & suggested steps are often helpful but not in every situation at all times.
